analysis.one_liner: Ends the oil and gas industry's exemption from federal drinking water rules for fracking.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote; it died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have removed a 2005 exemption that lets hydraulic fracturing — fracking — inject fluids underground without following the Safe Drinking Water Act rules that apply to everyone else. It would also have required companies to disclose which chemicals they pump into the ground during fracking, posted publicly online, with exceptions protecting proprietary formulas and an exception letting doctors get the formula in a medical emergency. The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near fracking wells — especially in places like Pennsylvania's Marcellus Shale — would gain the right to know what chemicals are being injected underground next to their water supplies, and their drinking water would fall under the same federal underground-injection protections as other industrial activity.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the Safe Drinking Water Act exemption for hydraulic fracturing, so fracking fluids injected near drinking water sources would be regulated as underground injection like other industrial fluids [S2] [S3].
It requires anyone using fracking to disclose the chemical constituents of their fracturing fluids to the state or EPA, and requires that the disclosures be posted on a public website [S3].

It lets a treating physician or nurse obtain a trade-secret chemical's identity immediately during a medical emergency, even without a prior written statement of need or confidentiality agreement [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies doing hydraulic fracturing would bear compliance costs — tracking, reporting, and publicly posting their chemical use — and would lose the regulatory carve-out they had operated under since 2005.

drawbacks.text: The industry's strongest objection was cost and delay: bringing every fracking well under Safe Drinking Water Act permitting could slow drilling in booming shale plays like the Marcellus, and drillers argued that states already regulated fracking adequately.

Even the bill's own disclosure rules leave a gap for industry: companies must reveal chemical constituents but not their proprietary formulas, so competitors' trade secrets stay hidden, and confidentiality agreements can still be required after an emergency disclosure.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit — knowing what is injected next to drinking water and closing a regulatory carve-out no other industry enjoys — is large for affected communities and costs the public little. The cost falls almost entirely on drillers, as slower permitting and compliance paperwork, and on no one else in any comparable way. The bill's main design weakness is that it still shields proprietary formulas, leaving part of the chemical picture hidden even if it had passed.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent it to the Environment and Public Works Committee on the day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed before the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Senator Casey introduced the bill on June 9, 2009, for himself and Senator Schumer [S3] [S5].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works, the last action ever recorded on the bill [S5] [S1].
The bill gathered 9 cosponsors — 8 Senate Democrats and the chamber's sole Independent — but never received a committee markup, hearing, or floor vote [S4] [S5].
The Congress ended January 3, 2011, and the bill expired without becoming law [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies came out ahead: fracking remained exempt from Safe Drinking Water Act underground-injection rules and chemical disclosure requirements throughout the fracking boom that followed, with no federal vote ever taken on the question.

for.name: Sen. Robert Casey Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sen. Charles Schumer
for.what_they_did: Joined Casey in introducing the bill.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never held a markup, hearing, or vote on it during the Congress.

against.name: American Petroleum Institute and oil and gas drillers
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against federal regulation of fracking under the Safe Drinking Water Act, arguing state oversight was sufficient and federal rules would slow drilling.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's lone Independent; no Republican signed on, and the Democratic-controlled committee never acted on the bill.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies using hydraulic fracturing
industries.note: The bill strips the industry's exemption from Safe Drinking Water Act underground-injection rules and requires public disclosure of its fracking chemicals, raising permitting and compliance costs. Its interest in keeping the exemption runs against residents' interest in knowing what is injected near their water.

industries.industry: Water utilities and public water systems
industries.note: Fracking fluids near drinking water sources would come under federal injection controls, reducing contamination risk that water systems and their customers otherwise bear.
